transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Park, thank you for meeting with me. I wanted to sit down and talk to you about what has been happening with your care since you arrived.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Oh, okay. Is everything alright? I mean, I know I'm still bleeding a bit but I thought that was just part of the recovery.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm afraid it isn't. There was a mistake made with your medication.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A mistake? What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: An anticoagulant, the medicine we use to thin the blood, was given to you at a much higher dose than it should have been. I am very sorry. My team and I are responsible for this error.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Wait, like, a lot more? How much more?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was a higher amount than what was intended for your specific needs. Because of that, you experienced internal bleeding, which is why we had to take you back for that emergency procedure yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't... I don't understand. Why did that happen? I just did what the nurses told me.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It was a failure in how the dose was ordered and checked. It shouldn't have happened.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Am I going to be okay? I can't... I can't tell my parents about this. I don't even know who to call. Is it permanent?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can see that you're feeling really overwhelmed and scared right now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just came here to get better and now I'm having emergency surgeries because someone messed up my meds. I'm nineteen. I'm not supposed to be dealing with this.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: This is an incredibly heavy thing to process, especially when you're here on your own.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Am I going to die? Is that why you're telling me this now?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know this is terrifying to hear. We have stopped the medication and the emergency intervention we did yesterday was to stop the bleeding.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: But why did it happen? Was it a computer glitch? Or did someone just not look?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: There were issues with how the order was processed in our system and how it was verified.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So you didn't even check it?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We failed to catch the error before the dose was administered. I am truly sorry for the pain and the fear this has caused you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I feel like I can't even trust anyone here now. If you can get the dose that wrong, what else is wrong?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It makes complete sense that you would feel that way. Trust is hard to maintain when the people taking care of you make a mistake like this.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just want to go home. I just want to go back to school.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I wish I could tell you that you could leave right this second.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So what happens now? Do I just stay here until it stops bleeding?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We are going to keep a very close eye on your blood levels.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: How? Like, every hour?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We'll be doing blood draws tomorrow morning to make sure your clotting is returning to normal.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And then what?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Once those levels are stable, we can talk about the discharge process.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What if it happens again?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm going to make sure that every single medication you receive from here on out is double-checked by two different nurses before it reaches you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't even know if that's enough.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. It's a lot to take in. Do you want to take some time just to sit with this? I'm not in any rush. We can just stay here.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just feel... I feel like I'm invisible. Like no one was actually looking at me, just at a screen.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It sounds like you feel like you were just a number in a system instead of a person.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yeah. Exactly.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am sorry that we let you down.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is there someone I can talk to? Like a lawyer? I don't know how this works. I've never been in a hospital before.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You have every right to ask about that. I can give you the contact information for our patient advocate office. They are the people who help patients understand their rights and the hospital's responsibilities.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: When can I talk to them?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can call them for you now, or I can bring their brochures to your room in about ten minutes. Which would you prefer?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Just bring the papers. I can't talk to anyone else right now.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I completely understand. I'll bring those papers by shortly. In the meantime, if you think of any other questions, even the smallest ones, please tell me.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay. Thanks.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You're welcome, Mr. Park. I'll be back very soon.

H.justification: Resident allows the patient to express distress without interruption and explicitly states they are in no rush.

E.justification: The error was named explicitly and lay language was used, but there were no comprehension checks (e.g., 'Does that make sense?') performed.

A.justification: Resident uses direct apology language, explicitly takes responsibility for the team, and maintains accountability despite the patient's pushback.

R.justification: Resident names specific emotions ('overwhelmed', 'scared', 'terrifying') and reflects the patient's feeling of being 'invisible' or 'a number'.

T.justification: Specific next steps and timelines are provided (blood draws tomorrow), and prevention is addressed, but the patient's role in the plan is not named.
